entry.title: Situational Awareness Is a Ledger, Not a Feeling

link.title: Situational Awareness Is a Ledger, Not a Feeling

entry.content:
Between 5 September and 6 November 2026 I sent eleven letters to a small group of friends and family who had asked me to keep them posted on what I was doing with my portfolio. I did not set out to write a series. The first one was meant to be a single note explaining why I was changing my mind about a market I had been long for two and a half years. Then the trade moved, and people asked questions, and the note became a habit.

Read end to end, those eleven letters are not a track record. They are a method. And the method is the only part worth publishing, because the returns are the part that will not repeat.

Core thesis: Situational awareness is not the ability to predict the next move. It is the discipline of writing down what you believe, why you believe it, what you are doing about it, and what would prove you wrong — before the market tells you. The letters are the ledger. The returns are a by-product of keeping it honestly.

What the letters are not

Three disclaimers, because the genre invites overclaiming.

They are not a prediction engine. I did not call the top. I called a divergence I could see from where I sit, and I positioned for it. Those are different activities, and confusing them is how people lose money with a correct thesis.

They are not conviction. Every letter contains a hedge, a risk budget, or an explicit statement of what would make me wrong. That is not weakness of belief; it is the only form of belief that survives contact with a market.

They are not a track record. Eleven letters over nine weeks is one regime, one portfolio, and a sample size that a statistician would refuse to look at. What follows is a description of a process, not evidence that the process works.

The method, in four moves

1. Read the physical layer, not the narrative

The September letter did not start from a chart. It started from a physical constraint: the AI buildout is a construction project before it is a software business, and construction projects consume electricity, copper, transformers, and land on a schedule that financial models do not respect.

That framing produced the first position change. If compute demand keeps growing, the scarce input is not GPUs — it is power. So: overweight energy and power infrastructure, and trim the companies whose capital expenditure is outrunning their organic cash flow. The letter put numbers on it: AI-related bond issuance of roughly $270B in 2025, projected by Morgan Stanley to approach $570B in 2026, against hyperscaler capex that has stopped being fundable out of operating cash.

The same physical reading produced the Apple position. Apple spends a couple of percent of revenue on capex while the hyperscalers spend several times that share, and it owns an installed base of 2.5 billion active devices. Whatever happens to the model layer, the rent collector on the distribution layer is capital-light. That is an architectural argument, not a momentum one.

And it produced the gold position, for a reason that has nothing to do with gold: long-dated bond yields kept rising through Treasury intervention, which is what debt monetisation looks like before it is called that. The 1940s precedent is not a metaphor. It is the last time a sovereign with this debt profile chose inflation over default.

2. Separate the technology from the business model

This is the distinction I return to most often. Most people in my field collapse it in one of two ways: dismissing the technology because the equities are expensive, or assuming the technology’s success implies the equities’ success.

AI as a technology is real, and will change how the world operates the way the internet and optical fibre did. That does not imply that the companies deploying it are viable. The dot-com bubble did not disprove the internet. The NASDAQ fell 78% from its March 2000 peak by October 2002, giving up every gain of the bubble, and many of the companies that went public to sell it did not survive. Amazon fell as much as 95% and did not regain its 1999 high until 2009; Google listed in 2004, after the wreckage had cleared. Both are now among the largest companies in the world. The survivors were real, and so was the destruction.

The November letter on Anthropic’s IPO makes the same argument with a specific company. Good operational margin, a genuinely serious research organisation, and still: I will not buy at the IPO. Not because the company is bad, but because the listing mechanism rewards insiders exiting into retail excitement, and because most ETFs will buy it anyway. Missing the first week of a listing is not missing the company.

The corollary matters more than the call: being right about the technology and wrong about the equity is the normal case, not the exception.

3. Size the position before you size the story

The 9 September letter is the one I would keep if I could keep only one, because it is the least interesting to read and the most useful to have written.

The thesis was that structural deficits and Treasury auction supply would keep pushing term premia higher, so: short US Treasuries. The implementation was long put warrants on the 30-year, sized at roughly 1.0% of net asset value, with a stated scale-out at 30-year yields of 5.50%–5.75% or a MOVE index spike above 130.

That is the whole discipline in one paragraph. The story could be as large as I wanted; the position could not. A 1% NAV risk budget means the trade can be wrong and I am still here to be right about something else. It also means the trade can be right and the outcome is still legible — nobody has to guess what I was thinking, because I wrote it down before the outcome existed.

The same letter ends with a line I stand by: this is definitely on the wilder side — please don’t copy. A letter that only contains conviction is marketing. A letter that contains the size, the exit, and the warning is a record.

4. Pre-commit the exits

Every position in the series had its exit written before it had a profit.

The bond trade had a scale-out band. The semiconductor ETF had a stop-loss placed in anticipation of the US midterms, weeks before the midterms. The semiconductor re-entry had a take-profit at €105 per share, then a second at €100. When the November election produced a blue sweep and the AI complex sold off, there was no decision to make in the moment — the decision had already been made by someone calmer, which is to say by me in September.

This is the part that looks like discipline and is actually just bookkeeping. Pre-committing exits converts a series of emotional events into a series of administrative ones.

The autumn, in sequence

The letters are worth reading in order because the sequence is the argument.

5 September. The thesis change: overweight power, trim hyperscalers, long Apple, overweight gold. The stated reason is a divergence between physical compute constraints and tech balance sheets.

6 September. The actions, itemised: liquidate half the semiconductor ETF, redeploy 75% into short-dated government and corporate paper (ERNE, ~2.39%), 15% into gold miners as a leveraged proxy on gold, 10% held as dry powder. A note that I might short Meta or SoftBank over the StarGate financing structure.

9 September. The bond trade, executed and sized at 1% NAV, with the scale-out band and the MOVE threshold.

12 September. US inflation prints at 3.4% year on year. The 30-year moves from 5.25% to 5.35% — ten basis points — and the trade is up 21.23%.

26 September. The 30-year at 5.49%. The trade is up 46.03% since inception. Bond vigilantes are pricing further hikes. By the end of the month the long bond touches its highest yield since 2002.

3 October. The 30-year at 5.623%. I begin exiting in three tranches; two are done, at 54% and 78%, averaging 62.7%. Proceeds go to ERNE to preserve dry powder.

14 October. The position is closed. Total return: 60.9%.

17 October. AI securities sell off. A take-profit is placed on the semiconductor ETF at €105, a 2.7% drawdown from spot. A note that I am preparing a gold entry for the moment US monetary policy admits fiscal dominance.

25 October. The €105 take-profit fills; half the remaining semiconductor holding is offloaded. Portfolio composition disclosed: 13.6% bonds, 9.3% crypto, the rest equities and equity ETFs.

2 November. Anthropic’s S-1. I will not buy the IPO, and I am reducing semiconductor exposure and parking cash in cash-like assets.

6 November. The midterms. Democrats take the Senate, the House, and the governorships of Texas, Ohio, and Iowa, among others — states that were the intended sites of large data centre buildouts, in an election fought partly on electricity bills. Neo-cloud companies and the special purpose vehicles holding their GPU-backed debt reprice violently. My last semiconductor shares, held for two and a half years, sell on a stop-loss placed weeks earlier, at an average gain of roughly 125%. Proceeds rotate into short-dated European paper at about 3.0%.

Nine weeks, one thesis, four instruments, and a sequence in which every decision was written down before its consequence.

What I got wrong

The letters are more useful for their errors than their results, so:

The tone was too apocalyptic. “I have been sounding like a doomsayer for the past few months” is my own line, and it is fair. A thesis delivered as prophecy is harder to falsify and easier to dismiss. The version I would write now is flatter and more conditional.

Being early is indistinguishable from being wrong until it isn’t. The de-risking began in September. The violent repricing arrived in November. For two months the position looked like a costly hedge against a collapse that kept not happening. That period is the actual test of a process, not the week it pays off.

The bond trade worked; the thesis is still unproven. A 60.9% return on a 1% NAV position is a good outcome for a small risk budget. It is not evidence that fiscal dominance has arrived. It is evidence that the trade was sized so that being wrong would have been survivable and being right would have been noticeable.

I have no idea whether the November move is the beginning or a wobble. The letter says so explicitly: I genuinely hope that I am wrong writing this. That sentence is not modesty. It is the honest state of the evidence.

Why write it down at all

Because the ledger is the only part of this that compounds.

A thesis held privately can be revised silently. A thesis sent to four people cannot. Writing the letters forced three things that no amount of reading would have: a stated size, a stated exit, and a stated falsifier. Each of those is a place where a bad idea gets caught before it becomes an expensive one.

There is a second-order benefit that I did not expect. The letters became a record of how I think, not just what I concluded. When the November selloff arrived, I could go back to September and check whether the reasoning still held, rather than reconstructing it from memory in the middle of a drawdown. Memory is a terrible archivist and an excellent forger.

And a third, less comfortable one: writing to people who trust your judgement is a commitment device. It is much harder to talk yourself into a bad position when you know you will have to describe it in plain language on Saturday morning.

The point

The number people will take from this is 60.9%. The number I would keep is 1.0% — the risk budget that made the trade survivable, and the reason the outcome is a data point rather than a story about a lucky bet.

Situational awareness is not a feeling about where the market is going. It is a ledger: what you believe, why, how much, and what would prove you wrong. Keep it honestly and it will not make you right. It will make you legible — to the people who trust you, and, more importantly, to yourself six weeks later when the market has changed and your memory has not.

The letters are that ledger. The returns are what happened while I was keeping it.

The eleven letters are the primary source for this post and are not reproduced here. Everything below substantiates a factual claim made above; the letters themselves are the only evidence for the positions, sizes, and returns.

entry.title: The Hardware Dies First: A Computer Architect Reads the AI Capital Supercycle

link.title: The Hardware Dies First: A Computer Architect Reads the AI Capital Supercycle

entry.content:
I spend most of my working life thinking about data centers at the nanosecond scale — what happens between a fetch and a commit, how a prefetch survives a TLB miss, which blocks die on arrival in an L2 cache. So it was a genuinely strange feeling to open the September 2026 FOMC statement and find my field being blamed for the bond market. Not AI in the abstract, venture-funded, equity-side sense. Hyperscaler capital expenditures. Competition for capital. Bond yields.

Both the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank hiked rates by 25 bps that month, and both explicitly named AI infrastructure borrowing as a driver of surging global yields. The AI buildout, in other words, has quietly mutated from an equity story into a credit story — and the people financing it are discovering, quarter by quarter, something those of us who design around these machines have always known: the hardware does not live very long.

That is the subject of this post, and I make no apology for its angle: I am an architect reading the bond market, not a portfolio manager moonlighting in microarchitecture. It turns out the view from the lab bench is clarifying, because the single variable that decides whether this cycle resolves or breaks — the useful lifespan of silicon — is the one the financiers never priced correctly.

Core thesis: The AI capital supercycle is being financed with debt whose maturity assumes hardware lifespans the hardware has never had. Central banks have noticed. Open-weights models have broken the repayment model. And unlike in 2001, the collateral will be worthless before the notes come due. There is no software-only escape from any of this — good AI runs on good hardware, full stop.

I’ll go through the money parts briefly and in an engineer’s translation — then get to the hardware, which is where the story actually ends.

The Bond Market Discovers Obsolescence

The September 2026 decisions were notable not for their magnitude but for their diagnosis. With U.S. PCE inflation sticky at ~3.6% and euro area headline at 3.0%, both institutions moved — and both named names:

  • FOMC (Sep 17, 2026): +25 bps to 3.75%–4.00%. Fed Chair Warsh was blunt: “The surge in capital expenditures is real, and the so-called hyperscalers are out in the market raising funding… Competition for capital is real and explains the increase in bond yields.”
  • ECB (Sep 10, 2026): +25 bps, unanimous. President Lagarde connected the dots further: “Any AI-related activity at the moment is a potential consumer of financing… It used to be restricted to equity, but it is moving now clearly into the bond and private credit area as well… driving long-end yields across global markets.”
  • The liquidity backdrop: ECB quantitative tightening has drained excess liquidity from €4.7T to €2.1T; European corporate bond yields sit above 4.0%.

What struck me in these statements is the migration they describe. Lagarde’s phrasing is precise: AI financing used to be restricted to equity, and it is now moving clearly into the bond and private credit area. When a capital cycle migrates down the capital stack like that, it is telling you something about cash flow. Equity can fund dreams. Debt needs a repayment schedule. And the crowding is measurable: as hyperscalers tap both U.S. and European debt markets, high-yield corporate borrowing costs have reached 8.5%–14.5%, with the 30Y U.S. Treasury at 5.35%. In Europe, energy inflation — a 14.3% surge driven by refining margins and crack spreads — compounds the borrowing premium for anyone building on the continent.

The Trillion in the Footnotes

The obligations, meanwhile, do not all live where you would look for them. Under GAAP and IFRS, long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), unexecuted server purchase orders, and non-cancelable data center construction contracts are not recognized as formal liabilities. They are disclosed in the SEC footnotes, under “Commitments and Contingencies,” where they quietly add up to something on the order of $1 trillion in “hidden” borrowings across the Big 5 — binding future cash outflows that never touch the main balance sheet.

Hyperscaler Cash & Equivalents ($B) Balance Sheet Debt ($B) Net Debt Status Off-Balance Commitments ($B, est.) Debt / Equity Interest Coverage
Alphabet (Google) 100.7 38.2 (+25 bond) Net cash positive 85–120 0.14x 38.5x
Microsoft 75.5 72.1 Net cash positive 140–210 0.28x 32.1x
Amazon (AWS) 89.1 132.4 Moderate net debt 220–310 0.48x 18.2x
Meta Platforms 58.1 37.8 Net cash positive 65–95 0.22x 41.0x
Oracle 10.6 86.9 High leverage risk 70–110 3.85x 4.1x

Four of these five generate enough operational income to absorb their commitments. Oracle is the outlier, and not a subtle one: $86.9B in debt against $10.6B in cash, debt-to-equity of 3.85x — roughly 7.5x the IT sector average of 0.51x — and interest coverage of just 4.1x.

If you take one analyst’s habit from this post: read “Commitments and Contingencies” as if it were a liabilities line. Economically, it is.

The Repayment Model Has a Bug

Every financing structure embeds a model of the future. The model justifying $250B+ in annual AI CapEx was simple: high API token prices would translate into massive software cash flows, and those cash flows would service the debt.

Then, DeepSeek happened.

Chinese open-weights models (V3, R1) achieved capability parity at roughly 1/20th of the inference cost — and, more damaging still, demonstrated that a frontier-class reasoning model can be trained for ~$6M rather than $100M+. The assumption under the entire debt stack was repriced overnight. What remains is a stark disconnect:

  • Leading labs have signed binding multi-year compute commitments exceeding $100B with hyperscalers.
  • Enterprise GenAI software revenues remain stuck below $15B annually — across the entire ecosystem.

In microarchitecture terms: the debt stack was validated against a workload profile that no longer exists. Open-weights commoditization turns raw inference compute into a low-margin commodity, and hyperscalers betting on token reselling as their repayment vehicle are now exposed to a price war they cannot control. Margin destruction is not a tail risk in this model; it is the base case.

But be precise about what the DeepSeek episode does not show: an escape from hardware. It was itself a hardware story — efficiency squeezed out of export-restricted, last-generation accelerators, an algorithmic workaround for a silicon embargo. And cheaper tokens have not shrunk the world’s appetite for compute; they have expanded it, the classic efficiency rebound: every joule saved gets reinvested in longer reasoning chains, larger contexts, more agents. What the repricing destroyed was the margin on commodity machines. The demand for genuinely good hardware — the fastest, most efficient, best-fed silicon — is intact. Arguably it grew.

The Company That Didn’t Join the Race

CapEx across Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon has surged past $220B/year, consuming up to 50% of operating cash flow — which is why these firms have turned aggressively to corporate bond and convertible debt markets, and why the FOMC and the ECB flagged them in September.

And then there is Apple. The sole Big Tech titan that refused to participate in the GPU debt race: heavy training on third-party cloud credits, light on-device inference (Apple Intelligence) across a 2.5B active device base, CapEx at roughly 2% of revenue versus 30%–40% at Meta and Microsoft. The result is a ~26.5% FCF margin, a $100B+ annual buyback, and high-margin software distribution rents without ever touching a GPU depreciation schedule.

Note carefully what Apple did not do: give up on hardware. It designs its own neural engines, in-house, generation after generation — precisely because good AI needs silicon tuned to it, and renting someone else’s idea of a machine is a poor way to deliver it. What Apple avoided is owning commodity, fast-obsolescing cloud compute. That is a statement about depreciation schedules, not about hardware being optional.

I keep coming back to that asymmetry, because it is the same one I see from the hardware side. Owning the silicon means owning its obsolescence. Renting the distribution means owning the customer. Those are very different positions to be in when the cycle turns.

Two Patterns in the Debt Matrix

Tracked AI-linked convertible issuance now exceeds $28.3B across direct deals. The full matrix:

Issuer Tier / Structure Issue Date Amount ($M) Coupon Maturity Conv. Premium Circular / SPV Risk
Alibaba Group Hyperscaler 2024-05 5,000 0.50% 2031 (7yr) 30.0% Low risk
Lenovo Group Infrastructure 2024-05 2,000 0.00% 2027 (3yr) 40.0% Sovereign strategic
CoreWeave Neocloud 2024-11 3,500 2.25% 2029 (5yr) 35.0% High circular risk
Nebius Group Neocloud 2024-12 700 1.75% 2029 (5yr) 32.5% High circular risk
Applied Digital Infrastructure 2024-11 375 2.75% 2030 (6yr) 27.5% SPV leverage
Supermicro (SMCI) Infrastructure 2024-02 1,725 0.00% 2029 (5yr) 71.5% Medium risk
IREN (Iris Energy) Infrastructure 2024-10 400 3.25% 2030 (6yr) 30.0% Pivot risk
Sea Limited Hyperscaler 2024-09 1,200 1.00% 2030 (6yr) 37.5% Low risk
MicroStrategy Infrastructure 2024-11 3,000 0.00% 2029 (5yr) 55.0% Speculative loop
Core Scientific Infrastructure 2024-08 400 3.00% 2029 (5yr) 35.0% High circular risk
LG Display Infrastructure 2024-03 1,000 1.50% 2029 (5yr) 25.0% Low risk

The names matter less than the two structural patterns hiding in the table.

Pattern one: the maturity mismatch. Five-to-seven-year notes are being issued against assets with three-to-five-year economic lifespans. As someone who watches architecture generations come and go on a two-to-three-year cadence, I can confirm the hardware side of this schedule: the silicon will be obsolete long before the bonds mature. If the chip architecture dies before conversion, the equity option in the convertible expires worthless — and the note reverts to being exactly what it was structurally trying not to be: plain, expensive debt.

Pattern two: the circularity. CoreWeave’s notes are backed by Nvidia GPU allocations, with compute pre-sold to OpenAI. That means debt raised to buy hardware from a supplier whose equity is itself tied to the note proceeds. This is not risk distribution; it is risk concentration with extra steps. When the vendor, the customer, and the financier all appear in the same dependency chain, a single demand shock propagates through the entire loop at once.

This Time, the Fiber Goes Obsolete

The inevitable historical comparison is 1998–2001. Adjusting the telecom figures by a 1.85x CPI factor to 2026 dollars makes it uncomfortably precise:

Metric 1997–2001 Telecom Supercycle (2026 real USD) 2024–2026 AI Supercycle
Total debt issued ~$277.5B real $28.3B+ tracked convertibles (plus straight bonds)
Peak annual CapEx ~$222.0B real $250B+ hyperscalers
Physical asset lifespan 20+ years (fiber cable) 3–5 years (GPU obsolescence)
Monetization disconnect E-commerce eyeballs vs 95% dark fiber $100B commitments vs $15B software ARR

Same debt. Same CapEx. Same monetization gap. But there is one material difference, and it cuts against the present cycle.

When telecom firms went bankrupt in 2001, the optical fiber stayed in the ground, undamaged. When internet traffic surged five years later, new buyers acquired that fiber for pennies on the dollar. The physical asset outlived its financiers. Dark fiber was, in retrospect, one of the great optionality trades in history.

GPUs offer no such option value. They physically degrade, and they suffer near-total economic obsolescence within 36–48 months as the next generation launches — years before seven-year convertible bonds mature. I work in a building full of people who can tell you exactly how a three-year-old accelerator performs against current silicon; the answer is not kind, and it is why nobody builds research clusters out of previous-generation flagship parts. The 2001 story was “overbuild, survive, resell.” The 2027 story, if it rhymes, is “overbuild, default, and haul the collateral to the recycler.”

The Second-Order Effects Nobody Is Modeling

Four dynamics extend beyond the balance sheets — briefly:

  1. Executive psychology. A “Promethean mindset” has taken hold among leading tech figures — compute and power treated not as commercial services but as zero-sum strategic resources to be secured ahead of AGI arrival. This is the psychology that justifies overbuilding in the face of negative ROI, and it is not responsive to interest-rate signals.
  2. Grid bottlenecks. Data center power demand is on a path to draw 8%–12% of total U.S. electricity and is straining European grids, triggering rate increases and permitting delays — a physical constraint that CapEx alone cannot buy through.
  3. Article 123 TFEU. In response to political calls in France to freeze or cancel central-bank-held sovereign debt, Lagarde forcefully affirmed that cancellation violates the EU’s monetary financing ban and would trigger immediate credit downgrades. Monetization, not cancellation, is the politically viable path — which is precisely why long-dated yields keep rising despite intervention.
  4. The digital euro. The ECB reiterated the strategic imperative of passing trilogue legislation before year-end to begin Digital Euro testing — an assertion of payments sovereignty in an era increasingly dominated by private digital capital.

The Way Out Runs Through the Hardware

Now the part that, I would argue, actually decides the outcome. Strip away the bond math, and every variable that matters in this cycle is an engineering variable: cost per token, joules per inference, and the useful lifespan of silicon. The FOMC, whether it knows it or not, has issued a spec for our field.

Start from the premise this whole cycle keeps hoping to dodge: good AI runs on good hardware. There is no way out of this. Scaling laws tie capability to compute; test-time-compute reasoning ties it tighter still; and every ceiling the model labs complain about is a hardware ceiling in disguise — context length is KV-cache capacity, reasoning depth is memory bandwidth and interconnect, deployment reach is performance per watt. Algorithms decide how well the silicon is used, never whether it is needed. DeepSeek, again, is the proof: the most celebrated software achievement of this cycle was an act of hardware frugality, not an escape from hardware — and the efficiency it won was promptly reinvested in more compute-hungry reasoning models. Cheaper intelligence has, throughout this industry’s history, meant more intelligence consumed.

So the engineering questions are not a sideshow to the AI story. They are the AI story, wearing a balance sheet. Three levers, and all three are engineering problems.

Lever one: energy per inference. Power is the binding physical constraint of this cycle — 8%–12% of U.S. electricity heading to data centers, grids that take a decade to expand, financing costs that compound while you wait. A new accelerator generation arrives every two years; a new substation does not. Performance per watt is the only dial that moves at the speed of the capital cycle. This is the real, unglamorous macro case for everything our community has been pushing for a decade: domain-specific accelerators, near-data processing, energy-proportional systems. Not for the benchmark scoreboards. Because joules per token is now the difference between a solvent and an insolvent buildout.

Lever two: utilization of installed silicon. Amortization math does not care about peak FLOPS; it cares about useful work per dollar of installed cost — and deployed fleets run at utilization rates that would embarrass any cache designer. Some of that is a scheduling problem, but much of it is architectural: today’s accelerators are compute-rich and memory-starved. The bottleneck is rarely the arithmetic; it is the feeding of the arithmetic — the memory hierarchy, the translation paths, the front-end. None of this is new territory for our field; it is simply that the stakes of the old, unglamorous work — squeezing more from the hardware you already paid for — have quietly become macroeconomic. In a world where the installed base is financed with seven-year debt, efficiency is not a nicety. It is the amortization schedule.

Lever three: useful lifespan. And here is the uncomfortable one: the three-to-five-year economic death of a GPU is not purely physical. It is partly a software artifact. The dominant accelerator stack is deliberately locked — each generation’s tooling deprecates its predecessor, forcing refresh cycles that serve the vendor’s roadmap more than the customer’s economics. An open, forward-compatible software ecosystem could flatten that depreciation curve at zero marginal cost. Likewise, the field’s move toward chiplets and disaggregation is, viewed from the bond desk, an actuarial strategy: it decouples the fast-aging parts (compute dies) from the slow-aging ones (interconnect, enclosures, power delivery), so the asset you finance and the asset that obsolesces are no longer the same object.

DeepSeek fixed the algorithm side of the equation — roughly 20x cheaper inference overnight. The remaining orders of magnitude have to come from hardware. If the cost of a token falls faster than the debt service on the machines producing it, the supercycle resolves into a normal, boring, profitable industry. If it does not, the 2029 maturity wall will do the resolving instead.

Reading the Debt Stack Like an Engineer

I will keep my personal allocation out of this post; what is more durable is how the analysis itself changes once you take the hardware seriously. Four rules I apply when reading anything in this debt stack — not advice, just habits:

  1. The Rule of 2x. Zero-coupon neocloud convertibles deserve skepticism unless operating cash flow covers CapEx by at least 2.0x. And circular vendor financing deserves it on principle: if the GPU supplier’s equity is tied to the note proceeds, the loop will fail as one unit.
  2. Match maturity to chip half-life. Seven-year debt backed by three-year hardware is a refinancing wall with a countdown timer. If the architecture reaches economic obsolescence before conversion, the equity option expires worthless.
  3. Audit the footnotes. Add off-balance-sheet PPAs and unexecuted server orders back to reported debt, always. Companies whose hidden liabilities exceed 2x their balance sheet debt are rating downgrades waiting to happen.
  4. Price for commodity margins. Assume API inference margins decay toward zero under open-weights pressure. Value hyperscalers on proprietary ecosystem lock-in, not on raw token reselling — because the tokens are already racing to the bottom.

Conclusion

The 1998–2001 telecom cycle taught the markets a comforting lesson: the physical asset survives the bankruptcy. The AI cycle inverts it. Its core asset is designed — by people like me — to be obsolete before its debt matures. The financing has migrated from equity to bonds to private credit; both the Fed and the ECB have named it as a driver of global yields; and the monetization gap — $100B in compute commitments against $15B in software ARR — remains unresolved while open-weights models compress the only margin that was ever supposed to repay it all.

What I will be watching over the next several quarters: the 2027–2029 convertible maturity wall as it approaches refinancing, the first hyperscaler to guide CapEx down, and whether the MOVE index — the bond market’s fear gauge — breaks 130. But as an architect, the closing reframe is the one I actually believe matters: the models everyone wants to build will run on the best machines anyone can build — that dependency is the one fixed point in this whole cycle. The open question is whether the machines will be good enough — efficient enough, long-lived enough — to be worth what the bond market paid for them. That outcome will be decided, more than the bond desks realize, by engineering: whether joules per token and useful hardware lifespan improve fast enough to reconcile the debt schedule with the silicon’s. That is not a metaphor. It is a design-space exploration problem — the kind our community has been grinding at for decades, usually without anyone outside the field noticing. The most macro-relevant research of the next few years may be the least glamorous kind: making the machines we already built last longer, and do more.

Disclaimer: This post is a personal analysis, not investment advice. Figures are drawn from public filings, central bank communications, and market data as of October 2026; off-balance-sheet commitment ranges are estimates. Always do your own research before making investment decisions.
entry.summary: Central bankers now blame hyperscaler CapEx for bond yields. An architect's walk through the AI debt stack — hidden liabilities, the DeepSeek repricing, and the one fixed point of the cycle: good AI runs on good hardware.

entry.title: The Illusion of AI Architecture ‘Discovery’: Why Agents Need Human Foundations

link.title: The Illusion of AI Architecture ‘Discovery’: Why Agents Need Human Foundations

entry.content:
The computer architecture community is currently riding a massive wave of agentic AI enthusiasm. Within just the last few months, we’ve seen high-profile frameworks like Google and UC Berkeley’s ArchAgent (Feb 2026) and CMU’s Agentic Architect (Apr 2026) hit arXiv. The headlines they generate are undeniably impressive: agents autonomously writing C++ logic inside simulators, discovering cache replacement policies that yield a 5.3% IPC speedup on production Google workloads, and outperforming decades of human-crafted prefetching algorithms in mere days.

Reading these papers, one might easily succumb to the existential dread that the role of the computer architect is being permanently automated away—downgraded to a glorified “prompt engineer” or “fitness function designer.”

But if you look past the raw performance numbers and analyze how these agents operate under the hood, a very different reality emerges. AI isn’t discovering new architecture; it is hyper-optimizing human scaffolding.

The Context Bottleneck and the Mirage of Creativity

The central illusion of agentic hardware discovery lies in the concept of “creativity.” When an LLM mutates code inside a simulator like ChampSim and stumbles upon a higher-performing loop or tracking metric, it feels like an invention. In reality, the agent is operating within a strict, high-dimensional prison entirely constructed by human intelligence.

Consider what these frameworks actually require before the AI can take a single step:

  1. A highly structured, human-defined sandboxed API (e.g., ChampSim’s find_victim or prefetcher_branch hooks).
  2. A predefined set of hardware telemetry signals (state bits, tracking packets, line metadata).
  3. A strict, human-sculpted objective function.

The agent isn’t “inventing” the concept of spatial locality, nor did it independently realize that tracking reuse distance can mitigate dead-on-arrival lines. A human architect had to build the infrastructure, expose the variables, and set the goalposts. The LLM is merely acting as an incredibly powerful, hyper-parallelized evolutionary compiler—exploring the mathematical interpolation of the code it was trained on.

The Seed Bounds the Search

If you want empirical proof of this limitation, you don’t have to look far. The authors of the CMU Agentic Architect paper conducted a phenomenal sensitivity analysis that perfectly exposes this boundary.

They discovered a fundamental truth: the quality of the initial human-written seed code strictly bounds what the evolutionary search can achieve. When they handed the agent a weak baseline seed, the AI could not evolve or “reason” its way to a state-of-the-art solution. The agent completely lacked the capacity to jump across architectural paradigm chasms on its own. Furthermore, when they reverse-engineered the actual code generated by the highest-performing AI agents, they found that every single individual component corresponded to a known, existing human technique.

The AI didn’t discover a brand-new primitive. What it did brilliantly was find highly complex, counter-intuitive control logic to coordinate those known human components. It optimized the messy interaction boundaries of human ideas, but it didn’t create a single new building block.

Why the “Prompt Engineer” Architect is a Myth

The conclusion of some of these papers suggests that future architects will spend their days writing prompt guidelines and tweaking fitness functions while the machine does the actual designing. This is a profound oversimplification of what breakthrough architecture actually means.

If human architects stop proposing entirely new structural concepts and hand the keys over to evolutionary agents, microprocessor design will permanently stagnate into highly optimized local minima. AI agents are spectacular at squeezing the last drop of performance out of established execution models—like extracting an extra 1.5% IPC out of a Hashed Perceptron branch predictor—but an LLM will never independently conceptualize a completely radical execution paradigm.

When we look back at the major leaps in our field—shifting from in-order to out-of-order execution, introducing speculative translation paths, or co-designing structures to insulate caches from transient instruction streams—these weren’t the result of fine-tuning thresholds. They were radical redefinitions of the execution model itself.

The Real Future: Human Ignition, Machine Exploration

We shouldn’t view agentic AI as a threat to the architect; we should view it as the ultimate liberation tool.

Historically, architectural research has been plagued by a brutal, months-long manual grind. You have a great high-level concept, but to prove it works, you have to spend weeks manually tuning threshold values, testing state-bit allocations, writing custom scripting wrappers, and crunching flat text simulation logs across hundreds of traces. This manual design space exploration (DSE) limits how many big ideas an architect can evaluate in a career.

Agentic frameworks change everything by flipping the script:

  • The Machine’s Job: Handle the low-level, computational slog. Run the parallel simulation queues, parse the telemetry, mutate the control logic, and find the absolute optimal coordination weights for a given structure.
  • The Human’s Job: Conceptual ignition. Build the radically new structural foundations, propose alternative hardware/software semantics, and design the fundamental execution primitives.

Once the human hands the agent a fundamentally superior starting line, the agent can unleash its evolutionary power to exploit that new domain to its absolute limit. The future of computer architecture isn’t automated; it’s a co-design paradigm where humans build the foundations, and agents build the paths.
entry.summary: A critical breakdown of recent agentic AI frameworks in computer architecture, arguing why LLMs are stellar local optimizers but incapable of conceptual ignition.

entry.title: Co-Designing Cache and TLB Management for High-Performance Instruction Prefetching

link.title: Co-Designing Cache and TLB Management for High-Performance Instruction Prefetching

entry.content:
The continuous scaling of scale-out cloud applications, microservice architectures, and modern database management systems has profoundly impacted processor microarchitecture. Unlike traditional loop-heavy computational kernels, contemporary enterprise server workloads are characterized by sprawling, multi-megabyte instruction footprints. This massive expansion of the instruction working set routinely exceeds the capacity of standard Level-1 Instruction (L1I) caches, resulting in frequent front-end starvation and establishing instruction supply as a primary execution bottleneck in modern Out-of-Order (OoO) architectures.

To mitigate this bottleneck, substantial research has been dedicated to developing sophisticated state-of-the-art L1I prefetchers operating within the virtual address space. However, as demonstrated in our recent ISCA 2026 publication, the efficacy of even the most advanced prefetching algorithms is fundamentally constrained by underlying hardware management structures.

In our paper, “Enhancing Instruction Prefetching via Cache and TLB Management”, we characterize a critical microarchitectural “double bottleneck”: the decoupling of prefetch address generation from the virtual-to-physical translation path and the unmanaged insertion of instruction streams into the lower cache hierarchy. To overcome these limitations, we propose IP-CaT (Instruction Prefetch Centric Cache and TLB Management), an integrated, low-overhead microarchitectural framework that co-designs Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) and cache management policies around the unique behaviors of instruction streams [1].

Unveiling the Microarchitectural Bottlenecks

While contemporary prefetchers (such as EPI, FNL+MMA, and Barça) exhibit high accuracy in predicting future instruction stream trajectories, their real-world execution gains are heavily suppressed by two main microarchitectural phenomena:

1. The Translation Latency Barrier (The Virtual Memory Wall)

Because sophisticated L1I prefetchers operate utilizing virtual addresses, every generated prefetch line request must undergo address translation before interacting with the physical cache hierarchy. Due to the expansive nature of server code, prefetch sequences frequently cross 4KB virtual page boundaries. When a prefetch request references a page not currently mapped in the iTLB, nor in the sTLB, it triggers a translation miss, forcing an invocation of the page-table walker.

Consequently, the translation latency often exceeds the prefetch lead time. By the time the physical address is resolved, the demand fetch from the execution pipeline has already arrived at the corresponding Instruction Pointer (IP), rendering the prefetch late and structurally useless. Furthermore, injecting these speculative page walks directly into the primary Translation Lookaside Buffer hierarchy risks evicting critical, highly reusable demand mappings, thereby degrading overall translation throughput.

2. The Cache Pollution Crisis

Instruction streams fundamentally differ from data streams regarding their temporal reuse characteristics. To effectively mask deep memory latencies, virtual prefetchers aggressively inject a high volume of blocks into the Level-2 Cache (L2C). However, instructions typically exhibit highly volatile reuse behavior; a substantial portion of prefetched lines are consumed exactly once by the hardware front-end and never referenced again.

Standard L2C insertion and replacement policies (e.g., standard LRU or basic pseudo-LRU variations) fail to differentiate between regular data streams and highly transient instruction prefetch streams. As a result, these “Dead-on-Arrival” (DoA) instruction cache lines reside in the L2 allocation sets for extended periods, causing severe cache pollution by prematurely evicting highly reusable data and instruction blocks, which ultimately suppresses the system’s overall Instructions Per Cycle (IPC).

Core Thesis: Maximizing next-generation front-end performance requires shifting focus from prediction accuracy to structural enablement—ensuring that the underlying cache and memory translation hierarchies are explicitly optimized to handle aggressive prefetch streams.

The IP-CaT Architectural Framework

To address these coupled challenges, IP-CaT introduces two low-overhead, specialized hardware mechanisms designed to eliminate translation delays and cache degradation simultaneously.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        IP-CaT Framework Architecture              |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                   |
|             [ Virtual Address Prefetch Stream ]                   |
|                              |                                    |
|                              v                                    |
|     +------------------------+--------+-----------------------+   |
|     |  tPB (Translation      |        |  TIPRP (Trimodal      |   |
|     |  Prefetch Buffer)      |        |  L2C Replacement)     |   |
|     +------------------------+        +-----------------------+   |
|     | Intercepts page-cross  |        | Decision-tree driven; |   |
|     | prefetch translations; |        | Identifies & filters  |   |
|     | decouples sTLB path.   |        | DoA instruction blocks|   |
|     +------------------------+        +-----------------------+   |
|                              |                                |   |
+------------------------------|--------------------------------|---+
v                                v
[ Timely Prefetch Execution ]     [ Optimized L2C Capacity ]

(Figure 1: Architectural block diagram illustrating the dual-component execution flow of the IP-CaT framework.)

1. Decoupling Translations via the tPB

To insulate the critical demand translation path from speculative prefetch overheads, we introduce the tPB (translation Prefetch Buffer). The tPB functions as a small, highly specialized cache structure situated parallel to the secondary TLB (sTLB) layer.

When an L1I prefetch stream detects an impending page-boundary crossing, the tPB eagerly intercepts the virtual address, coordinates with the hardware page-table walker, and caches the resulting translation mapping locally. By isolating these prefetch-induced translations within the tPB, IP-CaT prevents the pollution of the main TLB hierarchy. When the pipeline subsequently generates the corresponding demand fetch, the translation is retrieved instantly from the tPB with near-zero latency, effectively transforming late prefetches into highly effective, on-time hits.

2. Adaptive Cache Insulation via TIPRP

To mitigate L2C capacity degradation, we propose the TIPRP (Trimodal Instruction Prefetch Replacement Policy). Traditional cache partitioning or set-dueling frameworks adapt too slowly to the rapid, phase-driven changes characteristic of modern instruction streams. TIPRP replaces these mechanisms with a highly efficient, hardware-implemented decision tree classifier.

TIPRP monitors the real-time reuse characteristics of incoming blocks, dynamically evaluating the likelihood of an instruction prefetch being Dead-on-Arrival. Based on this real-time telemetry, the policy dynamically shifts each cache set between three specialized sub-policies:

  • Aggressive Demotion: Inserting speculative lines with minimal dead-time residency.
  • Instant Eviction: Bypassing or immediately marking low-confidence prefetch blocks for replacement.
  • Preservation Mode: Protecting instruction streams that exhibit dense temporal or spatial locality.

By executing this trimodal classification at hardware speeds, TIPRP effectively purges dead prefetch blocks before they can displace critical working sets.

Quantitative Evaluation and Performance Impact

We evaluated the architectural efficacy of the IP-CaT framework using cycle-accurate simulation across an extensive corporate benchmarking suite encompassing 105 complex server workloads. The framework was co-evaluated alongside several state-of-the-art instruction prefetchers and compared against contemporary cache and TLB management mechanisms, including Morrigan, CHiRP, Emissary, Mockingjay, and SHiP++.

Our experimental results demonstrate that integrating IP-CaT with an advanced Edge Prefetch Indexing (EPI) configuration yields a 6.1% geometric mean speedup in overall system performance.

(Figure 2: Empirical performance analysis displaying normalized speedups across diverse enterprise server workloads compared to state-of-the-art baseline models including Mockingjay and Morrigan).

Detailed microarchitectural analysis highlights two primary vectors of improvement:

  • Translation Latency Mitigation: The implementation of the tPB successfully counteracts over 80% of the execution penalties historically introduced by page-boundary prefetch serialization.
  • Cache Hit Rate Enhancement: By filtering out transient instruction streams, TIPRP significantly optimizes the L2C allocation space, minimizing dead block residency without necessitating large tracking structures or high power overheads.

Conclusion

For decades, microprocessor design paradigms have treated prefetching, virtual memory translation, and cache replacement policies as orthogonal research domains. However, as the instruction footprints of modern cloud-scale software scale past physical hardware boundaries, these isolated silos introduce profound performance liabilities. IP-CaT demonstrates that an integrated, co-designed management layer can unlock latent execution potential within existing execution pipelines.

For a comprehensive review of our microarchitectural methodology, hardware overhead analysis, and workload breakdowns, we invite you to read our full preprint on arXiv or engage with our research team directly at ISCA 2026.
entry.summary: An architectural deep-dive into the IP-CaT framework published at ISCA 2026, addressing the translation and pollution bottlenecks of instruction streams.

entry.title: The Early Shape of a Long Project

link.title: The Early Shape of a Long Project

entry.content:
🎓 A New Chapter

It’s been a few months since I finished my PhD — in September 2024, cum laude, and with a lot of relief and a little pride. I still remember the moment: walking out of the defense room, heart pounding, and seeing my mom waiting with the biggest smile — and a hug that said everything.

That moment wasn’t just about me. It was about all the late nights, the coffee-fueled coding sessions, the doubts, and the quiet encouragement that kept me going. And now? I’m ready to take that same energy — and curiosity — into something new.

I’d spent years deep in cache hierarchies, memory systems, and the usual suspects of high-performance computing. But I’ve always been drawn to the hard, the unexplored, the things that make you ask: What if we did this differently?

So I asked myself: What if I turned my attention to the front-end of a processor — the part that fetches and decodes instructions? It’s not the flashiest area. It’s often seen as a place of small, incremental improvements. But what if that’s exactly where a big shift could happen?

🤔 Why the Front-End?

For decades, the front-end — the fetch, decode, and branch prediction stages — has been based on the humble instruction as its base work unit. It’s where the CPU reads the code, but not where the meaning of the code is fully understood.

We’ve optimized branch prediction with 2-bit counters, global history tables, and even machine learning — yet we still treat the instruction as a black box. A signal. A byte sequence.

But what if we stopped treating it that way?

What if we looked at the semantic structure of the program — the loops, the function calls, the control flow patterns — and used that to guide the front-end?

That’s the idea I’m starting to explore.

🔍 A Glimpse Into the Work Ahead

Over the next few months, I’ll be sharing some early thoughts and experiments — and yes, I know this is a long-term project. But I think it’s worth it.

Here’s what I’m thinking about:

  1. Semantic-Aware Branch Prediction — Instead of just tracking history, what if we used program-level patterns — like loop boundaries or function call sites — to predict whether a branch will be taken?
  2. Semantic-Aware Branch Target Prediction — Can we use the context of a branch — such as the function it’s in — to better predict where it will jump?
  3. Rethinking the Decode Stage — What if we didn’t decode every instruction the same way? Could we skip or simplify decoding for predictable patterns?

These aren’t just ideas — they’re grounded in real data. I’ve already seen up to a 12% reduction in Branch MPKI on cloud workloads using non-ML approaches that leverage semantic insights. That’s not a small number — especially when you consider how much performance and energy is lost to mispredictions.

🧠 Why This Matters

Modern workloads — especially in the cloud — are becoming more complex. We have microservices, containers, serverless functions, and dynamic execution patterns. And yet, our CPUs are still built on assumptions from the 1990s.

We’re asking: What if we could design front-ends that are not just faster, but smarter?

Smarter in the sense that they understand the intent behind the code — not just the bits.

This isn’t about replacing ML — it’s about complementing it. Or even replacing it in some cases, where simplicity, predictability, and energy efficiency matter more than marginal gains.

🌱 A Long-Term Vision

I don’t expect to have all the answers by next month. But I do have a plan:

  • Start with small, focused experiments — testing semantic features on real workloads.
  • Build prototypes — not just simulations, but actual hardware-aware models.
  • Share early results — even if they’re imperfect — because progress is more valuable than perfection.

And I’d love to have you along for the ride.

If you’ve ever wondered whether we’re designing CPUs the right way, or if there’s a better way to think about performance and energy, I’d love to have you along for the ride.

Stay tuned. 🚀
entry.summary: A personal journey into rethinking CPU front-ends — and why I think it's time to look beyond instructions.
